To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the European Court of Human rights ruled that indefinite detention of those convicted of violent crimes is only lawful if there is evidence of rehabilitation.

there is a violation of Article5(1) of the European Convention of Human Rights if a person serving a sentence of Imprison for Public Protection is not provided with suitable rehabilitative provisions.

the European Court of Human rights has recently held that the UK has violated the European Convention of Human Rights by failing to provide rehabilitative provisions to prisoners serving indeterminate sentences.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following question: how can the European Court of Human Right’s jurisprudence be used to challenge the ongoing injustice of Imprisonments for Public Protection?
whether the abolition of IPP sentences will be sufficient to address the ongoing injustices of indefinite detention.
whether the Court's ruling is compatible with the current legal and policy landscape in the UK, and, if not, what the implications are for the Government's recent abolition of IPP.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the Court's approach is not only consistent with the principle of legality, but is also a necessary and proportionate measure in the context of the risk‐based sentencing regime that currently prevails in the United Kingdom.
the European Court of Human rights has made it clear that the UK government cannot continue to imprison people without a rehabilitative purpose.
the Court’s approach to indeterminate sentences is not only a welcome development, but is also consistent with the approach of the Court to other areas of criminal justice.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Court has not ruled that indefinite detention is incompatible with human rights, but has rather ruled that indefinite detention without rehabilitation is incompatible with human right.
the Court’s ruling is a significant step towards ensuring that indeterminate sentences do not breach the right to liberty.
the ECHR has now established that the imposition of an indeterminate sentence is not in itself a breach of Article 5.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in the absence of rehabilitative provisions, indeterminate detention for public protection may be incompatible with Article 5(4).
the Court's jurisprudence on this point is inconsistent and, in any event, the Court's approach is unsatisfactory.

the Court’s jurisprudence is highly relevant to the current debate on risk and sentencing, as it provides a useful framework within which to evaluate whether indeterminate sentences can ever be compatible with Article 5(4) of the ECHR.
